newsitem.title: GERMANY: E.Europe could export grain to Mediterranean - Toepfer.
newsitem.headline: E.Europe could export grain to Mediterranean - Toepfer.

text.p: With large grain harvests in prospect this year, several Eastern European grain producing countries could export surpluses to countries around the Mediterranean, grain and feeds merchant Toepfer International said on Saturday.
It put the combined grain surplus from eastern and central Europe including the CIS at 15 million tonnes but stressed logistical problems would make actual exports of that size impossible.
The comments were made in a company report on activities in the Dec/Nov 1995/96 fiscal year.
Toepfer singled out Ukraine, Russia and Kazakhstan for large grain crops while domestic feed grain demand was due to fall as livestock numbers were declining.
World grain harvests were generally looking ample this year and this had reduced soft red winter wheat prices to $120 a tonne from $147 last December, Toepfer said.
But soybean supply was tight and global demand still rising so United States and Latin American producers would need to harvest huge crops in 1997 and 1998.

European Union meals and feeds imports were seen declining because of competition from domestic feedgrain. EU feeds imports in 1996 totalled 37 million tonnes versus 40 million the year before and 44 million in 1994.

Toepfer in 1995/96 raised its turnover by 12 percent to 10.3 billion marks from 9.2 billion in 1994/95. Sales volume from headquarters and 43 subsidiaries worldwide dropped four percent in 1995/96 to 35.9 million tonnes.
The company result had been excellent due to higher prices, Toepfer said without specifying further.
The 1996/97 season started with good sales but falling commodity prices caused a fall in long-term ordering later -- consumers covered only nearby requirements and margins fell.

Toepfer said the centre of its activities was still European feeds and seeds imports as well as grain exports. But offices in Latin America, Asia and the U.S. were already employing more than half of the total staff of 947. North Africa, the Middle East and eastern Europe were also gaining importance.
